connection: Sessions 01 and 02 scaffolded the learner solution and established its dependency direction. This session writes the first purposeful statements in its console application and uses the build-run-test loop to observe how names, types, literals, conversions, and expressions produce values.
objectives: Describe a variable as a typed name bound to a value, not as an untyped box.
Distinguish declarations, literals, conversions, and expressions.
Choose decimal for deliberate base-10 quantities and recognize when a conversion is explicit.
Predict the value and type produced by a small numeric expression.

visuals.title: A name carries a type contract
visuals.explanation: The variable name hours makes intent visible, while its declared type limits which values and operations are valid.

visuals.title: Expressions produce values
visuals.explanation: Operands and operators are evaluated to produce a result. The result can be assigned, passed, returned, or observed.

visuals.title: Types control valid operations
visuals.explanation: A value must fit the target type. When types differ, C# either applies a permitted implicit conversion or requires an explicit cast.

visuals.title: Decimal models base-10 quantities
visuals.explanation: decimal is useful when base-10 precision is part of the domain. The m suffix makes a numeric literal a decimal value.

preQuiz.prompt: What does the m suffix mean in 8m?
options: The value is measured in meters
preQuiz.explanation: The suffix tells the compiler to treat the literal as decimal.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does converting TotalHours to decimal require an explicit cast?
options: TotalHours is a double and the conversion can change representation
preQuiz.explanation: double and decimal use different representations, so C# requires the programmer to acknowledge this conversion.

preQuiz.prompt: If recordedHours is 8m and scheduledHours is 7.5m, what does recordedHours - scheduledHours produce?
preQuiz.explanation: Subtraction evaluates both decimal operands and produces a decimal result.

concept.title: Declarations create typed names
paragraphs: A declaration connects a type, a name, and usually an initial value. The type is a compile-time contract: it determines which values can be assigned and which operations are available.
Names should explain the role a value plays. targetHours communicates more than x even when both have the same type.

concept.title: Expressions are evaluated
paragraphs: An expression is code that produces a value. A literal such as 6.5m is an expression; so are a variable read, a method call, and subtraction.
Evaluation happens before assignment. In difference = currentHours - targetHours, subtraction produces a value and that result is assigned to difference.

concept.title: Conversions should be visible when meaning changes
paragraphs: A measurement-oriented source may provide double while a base-10 business calculation uses decimal. Moving between them requires an explicit conversion.
The cast is not a promise of extra accuracy. It is a visible change of numeric representation. Later APIs such as TimeSpan.TotalHours create this same decision.

lab.objective: Calculate and display the difference between scheduled and recorded hours using typed numeric variables.
lab.startingCondition: Continue in the learner workspace scaffolded in Sessions 01–02. Open src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/Program.cs. Because the project came from dotnet new console, the file contains only Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!");. No TimeClock models or completed application code exist yet.

steps.text: From the learner workspace root, open src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/Program.cs. Confirm it contains the console template's Hello, World! line, then remove that line so you can build the exercise in the empty file.

Begin with one supplied measurement value. Add double measuredHours = 8.0;. This represents eight recorded hours arriving in a measurement-oriented type and gives the later conversion a visible source.

Before adding the remaining variables, write your predictions in a notebook or temporary comment. scheduledHours will be decimal 7.5, recordedHours will be measuredHours converted to decimal, and varianceHours will mean recorded minus scheduled. Predict each value and type so the run can test your reasoning.

reveals.title: Expected reasoning
items: scheduledHours should be decimal 7.5 because it will use the literal 7.5m.
recordedHours should be decimal 8.0 because converting measuredHours changes its type, not its visible value.
varianceHours should be decimal 0.5 because recorded minus scheduled is 8.0 - 7.5.

steps.text: Declare scheduledHours explicitly as decimal and assign 7.5m. The m suffix matters because a fractional literal is double by default; this schedule is deliberately a base-10 value.

reveals.title: Common mistake
reveals.text: decimal scheduledHours = 7.5; does not compile because 7.5 is a double literal. Add m to make the literal decimal.

steps.text: Convert measuredHours from double to decimal and assign the result to an explicitly typed recordedHours variable. Keep the cast beside measuredHours so the representation change is visible.

reveals.title: Common mistake
reveals.text: Removing (decimal) causes a conversion error because C# does not implicitly assign a double value to decimal.

steps.text: Create varianceHours by subtracting scheduledHours from recordedHours. Read the expression aloud as recorded minus scheduled, then compare the result with your written prediction.

reveals.title: Why order matters
reveals.text: Reversing the operands still compiles, but produces -0.5 and changes the meaning to scheduled minus recorded.

steps.text: Write three Console.WriteLine statements that display scheduledHours, recordedHours, and varianceHours. Format the first two with F2. Use +0.00;-0.00;0.00 for variance so positive, negative, and zero values are distinguishable. Try writing the statements before revealing the answer.

reveals.title: Expected code

steps.text: Run the console project and compare each value with your written prediction. Then test the solution. Success means the three numeric values match and the scaffolded test project still passes.
steps.code:
dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj --configuration Release
dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

reveals.title: Expected output
reveals.text: The labels may differ slightly if yours are equally clear, but the values should be:
reveals.code:
Scheduled hours: 7.50
Recorded hours: 8.00
Variance hours: +0.50

reveals.title: Common validation mistakes
items: A build error mentioning double and decimal usually means the m suffix or explicit cast is missing.
A variance of -0.50 means the subtraction order is reversed.
A remaining Hello, World! line is harmless but should have been removed to keep the output focused.
Different spacing is harmless; the values and passing tests are what matter.

lab.expectedBehavior: The console reports 7.50 scheduled hours, 8.00 recorded hours, and a +0.50 variance. The student's written predictions match those values, the application exits normally, and the scaffolded tests pass.
lab.validation: dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Add typed numeric values, an explicit conversion, and observable expressions.
Publish the synchronized lesson, scaffolded lab, hidden guidance, and quizzes.

commit: session-03: teach variables expressions and numeric types
review: Each variable name describes its role in the calculation.
Decimal literals use the m suffix.
The double-to-decimal conversion is explicit and close to its source.
The variance expression has an unambiguous subtraction order.
Output formatting does not change the stored numeric values.
The solution builds without warnings and all tests pass.

postQuiz.prompt: The output shows +0.50. Where is the plus sign introduced?
options: By the custom numeric format used for display
postQuiz.explanation: Formatting controls the text representation; the stored decimal value is still 0.5m.

postQuiz.prompt: What changes if scheduledHours becomes 8.5m while recordedHours remains 8m?
postQuiz.explanation: The expression is recorded minus scheduled, so a larger schedule produces a negative result.

postQuiz.prompt: Why not declare every numeric value as var in this lesson?
options: Explicit types keep the numeric contract visible while the concept is being learned
postQuiz.explanation: Type inference is useful, but explicit types make this lesson's conversions and numeric choices easier to inspect.

reflections: Which parts of the new statements are expressions?
What information does decimal communicate that the variable name alone does not?
Does formatting a value to two decimal places change the value or only its text representation?
whatBreaks: Removing scheduledHours leaves no comparison target. Removing the explicit conversion prevents assignment from double to decimal. Reversing the subtraction changes the meaning of positive and negative variance even though the code still compiles.
summary: Variables are typed names for values. Expressions produce values, literals have types, conversions change representation, and formatting changes only how a value is displayed.
